sentences.text: The only known specimen consists of the back part of a skull along with six teeth and four vertebrae.
This skull is sturdy and moderately tall, yet it is wider than it is high, featuring a flattened snout.
A raised dome sits before the eyes, formed by several bones, while the top of the skull has an hourglass shape.
The bone surface shows small circular pits and ridges, particularly on the cheekbone and the upper skull table.
The preserved teeth are blunt and rounded with an oval cross-section, standing low relative to their height.
These teeth are slightly flattened on the sides, bear lines near the base, and show a ridge on at least one tooth but lack serrations.
The overall skull shape closely matches that of modern gharials and freshwater crocodiles.
Grooves on either side of the olfactory tract gave the top of the skull a vaulted appearance.
The angle between the forebrain and midbrain forms a 170° turn, whereas the shift to the hindbrain creates an angle of roughly 120°.
Well-developed air pockets within the skull resulted from an expanded system of paratympanic sinuses.
The entire animal may have reached a length of about 4 meters.
Its eyes were positioned high on the skull and angled upward, allowing them to stay above water while the rest of the head remained submerged.
Fossils were unearthed in 2000 near Monte Alto County within the Serra do Jabuticabal escarpment of the Bauru Basin.
The genus was first described by Fabiano Vidoi Iori and Karina Lucia Garcia in 2012.
The species name honors paleontologist Cledinei Aparecido Francisco for his technical support during the excavation.
The fossil was found near a cave where the snout had already been eroded away before discovery.
Barreirosuchus is thought to have been semiaquatic, living similarly to modern crocodilians.
The shape of the postorbital bar helped create skull depth by distancing the skull roof from the jugal bone.
The genus contains only one species, Barreirosuchus franciscoi, which serves as the type species.
It belongs to the family Itasuchidae, a group it shares several shared derived traits with Caririsuchus camposi and Itasuchus jesuinoi.
Taxonomically, Barreirosuchus is classified within the class Reptilia.
This extinct genus lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically from the Campanian to Maastrichtian stages, between 83.6 and 66 million years ago.
Remains were found in the Late Cretaceous deposits of São Paulo State in southeastern Brazil.
A detailed redescription including internal anatomy via CT scans was published by Fachini and colleagues in 2025.
